skill.name: ai-agents-architect
skill.description: Design autonomous AI agents with suitable loops, tools, memory, planning, recovery, observability, and multi-agent coordination.
skill.summary: Create controllable agent architectures with practical patterns for tools, memory, planning, recovery, and evaluation.
skill.author: sickn33

content.value_statement: Autonomous agent projects often fail through weak controls, unclear tools, and unsuitable architecture. This skill guides practical designs for planning, memory, recovery, orchestration, and observability.
actual_capabilities: Selects between ReAct, plan-and-execute, supervisor, and tool registry patterns.
Defines iteration limits, timeouts, cost caps, and tool failure controls.
Structures working, episodic, and semantic memory with retrieval guidance.
Designs focused tool specifications with parameters, examples, and expected errors.
Plans checkpoint recovery, tracing, evaluation, and debugging for long-running agents.
Assesses when specialist agents justify multi-agent coordination overhead.
limitations: Provides architecture guidance, not a complete runnable agent implementation.
Does not replace framework documentation, environment testing, or security review.
Requires clear goals, available tools, permissions, and operational constraints.
Does not provide benchmark results or guarantee agent reliability.

use_cases.title: Design a First Tool-Using Agent
use_cases.description: Choose an agent loop, define focused tools, and add practical limits for a bounded application workflow.

use_cases.title: Plan a Long-Running Agent Platform
use_cases.description: Structure memory, checkpoints, recovery, and observability for agents that maintain task progress across failures.

use_cases.title: Review Agent Reliability
use_cases.description: Identify uncontrolled loops, silent tool errors, excessive memory, brittle parsing, and unnecessary multi-agent complexity.

prompt_templates.title: Choose an Agent Pattern
prompt_templates.prompt: Design an AI agent for [task]. Compare ReAct and plan-and-execute, then recommend one with required tools, limits, and failure conditions.

prompt_templates.title: Specify Tools and Controls
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a tool plan for an agent that handles [workflow]. Define each tool purpose, parameters, errors, retries, permissions, and execution limits.

prompt_templates.title: Design Memory and Recovery
prompt_templates.prompt: Architect memory and checkpoint recovery for [long-running task]. Separate working, episodic, and semantic memory, with retention, retrieval, cleanup, and resumption rules.

prompt_templates.title: Evaluate a Multi-Agent System
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this proposed multi-agent system: [architecture]. Assess role boundaries, handoffs, supervisor logic, failure recovery, observability, cost, and whether one agent is sufficient.

output_examples.input: Design a support agent that searches documentation and drafts answers.
output: Pattern: ReAct with a maximum of six tool iterations.
Tools: documentation search, article retrieval, and answer submission.
Controls: citation requirements, timeout handling, and human review for uncertain answers.

output_examples.input: Plan recovery for a research agent that may run for several hours.
output: Checkpoint after each completed research section.
Store task progress separately from retrieved source summaries.
Resume from the latest valid checkpoint and clear temporary data after completion.

output_examples.input: Decide whether a content workflow needs multiple agents.
output_examples.output: Start with one agent using focused research, drafting, and review tools. Add specialists only when measured failures show that role separation improves results.

best_practices: Set iteration, token, time, and cost limits before enabling autonomous execution.
Give every tool a clear purpose, typed parameters, examples, permissions, and recoverable error responses.
Trace decisions, tool calls, latency, token usage, checkpoints, and final outcomes.
anti_patterns: Do not run agent loops without explicit stopping conditions and circuit breakers.
Do not store every observation or expose large tool catalogs without relevance filtering.
Do not introduce multiple agents before one well-equipped agent demonstrates measurable limitations.

faq.question: Which agent patterns does this skill cover?
faq.answer: It covers ReAct, plan-and-execute, tool registries, hierarchical memory, supervisor coordination, and checkpoint recovery.

faq.question: Does this skill generate runnable code?
faq.answer: It focuses on architecture and design guidance. Implementation still depends on your language, framework, models, and infrastructure.

faq.question: Can it help define agent tools?
faq.answer: Yes. It guides tool purpose, selection, parameter documentation, examples, error handling, retries, and focused tool sets.

faq.question: How does it address runaway costs?
faq.answer: It recommends iteration limits, token limits, timeouts, cost caps, and circuit breakers for repeated tool failures.

faq.question: When should I use multiple agents?
faq.answer: Use them when independent specialist roles provide measured benefits that justify coordination, debugging, latency, and cost overhead.

faq.question: Does it cover production monitoring?
faq.answer: It recommends structured tracing for actions, tool inputs, outputs, errors, token usage, latency, and recovery events.
